title: RAG is not retrieval — it is a knowledge architecture question
excerpt: Most RAG discussions get stuck on chunking strategies. The important questions are about how you model knowledge.
body:
Most discussions of retrieval-augmented generation get stuck early. They debate chunk sizes, embedding models, similarity thresholds, and reranking strategies. These are real engineering questions, but they are downstream of a more fundamental one: how do you model knowledge in a way that makes the right information retrievable at the right level of granularity?

The knowledge modelling problem

RAG works by finding semantically related content and injecting it into the model's context. The quality of what gets retrieved depends entirely on how knowledge was structured when it was ingested. If your source documents are inconsistently formatted, poorly delineated, or lack the metadata needed to discriminate between related but distinct concepts, no retrieval strategy will save you.

I have seen teams spend weeks tuning embedding models while ignoring the fact that their source documents were 200-page PDFs with no logical section boundaries. The retrieval layer was returning paragraph-level noise from randomly sliced text. The problem was not the retriever — it was that nobody had modelled the knowledge.

What knowledge modelling actually involves

Before you write any RAG code, you need answers to several questions: What are the natural units of knowledge in your domain? How do those units relate to each other? What metadata is needed to filter retrieved results by recency, authority, or relevance to context? What does a retrieval failure look like, and how will you detect it?

These are information architecture questions as much as they are engineering questions. The teams that build RAG systems that work reliably in production are the ones that treat knowledge design as a first-class concern — not a preprocessing detail.
